name_en: Huangshan Mao Feng (Yellow Mountain Fur Peak)
processing: Baked green (hong qing): a brief wither, pan-firing to kill the green, very light rolling that keeps the shoot whole, then drying in two or three stages over charcoal or in a dryer; no pressing or heavy shaping.
harvest_season: Spring only, late March to mid April for the top grades; special grade is picked around Qingming, lower grades run into early May.
appearance_dry: Slightly curved, plump bud-and-leaf shoots like sparrow tongues, ivory-tinged yellow-green with fine down and a small golden 'fish leaf' at the base.
appearance_wet: Fat, soft yellow-green buds with one or two leaves, whole and even.
taste_profile: Orchid-like florals and a mild chestnut sweetness on a soft, round body; gentle and long rather than brisk.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan or glass. Forgiving by green-tea standards: it tolerates slightly hotter water than Longjing or Biluochun, and the baked style rewards a fourth steep.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest in grades: special grade (bud with one leaf just opening, picked around Qingming), then grades 1 to 3 picked later in April and early May. Only spring tea is sold under the name; summer leaf goes into other products. Buy fresh in April–May and drink within the year; kept cold and sealed it holds up a little better than pan-fired greens.
description:
Huangshan Mao Feng is the baked green tea from the hills around Yellow Mountain in southern Anhui, and it is the gentle one: where Longjing is toasty and Biluochun is brisk, Mao Feng is soft, floral and sweet. The name means 'fur peak', for the downy buds shaped like tiny peaks. The tea merchant Xie Zheng'an is credited with creating the style in 1875, which makes it one of the younger famous teas.

What sets it apart is the finishing. After a quick pan-firing the shoots are barely rolled, so they keep their plump shape, and then they are dried slowly with warm air instead of being pressed in a wok. That baking is why the leaf keeps its ivory tone and its golden fish leaf (the tiny first scale at the base of the shoot, a marker of the real thing), and why the flavour is round and orchid-like rather than roasted.

Across steeps it starts floral and sweet, picks up mild chestnut in the second, and fades to a clean, cool sweetness by the fourth. It is one of the more forgiving greens: 80–85 °C is fine, a gaiwan gets more out of it than a glass, and it does not punish a slightly long steep. Low-grade lots can taste flat and hay-like, usually a sign of late picking or tired leaf rather than bad making.

Grades are the thing to understand when buying. Special grade is picked around Qingming, bud with one leaf, ivory-yellow and even; grade 1 is one bud with one or two leaves; by grade 3 the leaf is bigger and the tea is a daily drinker. The Huangshan name covers a wide area and a lot of Anhui 'mao feng' from outside it, so ask for the county or village (Fuxi in Huizhou district is where the style began, and Gangcun and Chongchuan near the mountain are well regarded) and look for the golden fish leaf.

If you drink it and want more aroma, Taiping Houkui from the same mountain range is the obvious next step; if you want more roast, Lu'an Gua Pian.
history:
For so famous a tea, Huangshan Mao Feng has a precise and fairly recent starting point. The credit goes to Xie Zheng'an, a Huizhou merchant from a once-comfortable family who was driven by war into the hills at Fuxi, then in Shexian and now in Huizhou district. In 1875, by the standard account, he and his family tended tea gardens there, picked shoots shaped like sparrow tongues and sent a batch to sell in Shanghai. The name is explained by the down on the leaf and the peak-like tips of the buds.

That makes it younger than many of its neighbours on the famous-tea lists, though the mountain area already had tea. The best-regarded gardens are usually named around the Huangshan scenic area and nearby villages such as Gangcun and Chongchuan.

Its modern fame was built up by state recognition. It is reported as being named among the top ten teas by the China Tea Company in 1955, was recognised as a famous tea by the Ministry of Commerce in 1982, and was chosen as a Foreign Ministry gift tea in 1986. It still turns up on nearly every list of China's famous teas, and shop-grade lots today often show far less down than the description promises.
